name: Wolff's law facial loading

lead: Wolff's law is a nineteenth-century principle that bone adapts its structure to the loads placed on it. In looksmaxxing it is the reasoning behind mewing, chewing, thumb pulling and bonesmashing: if bone responds to load, then loading the face should build a stronger jaw and more prominent cheekbones.

The general principle, now usually called bone functional adaptation, is supported by research on limbs and the spine. Bone cells sense strain and signal bone-forming and bone-resorbing cells, and Frost's mechanostat model describes strain thresholds for adding or losing bone. Whether the small, specific forces of tongue posture, chewing or pulling change the adult facial skeleton has not been tested.

paras: People apply it by choosing practices that load the face, such as tongue posture, hard chewing or pulling on the palate, and by tracking changes in photos. It is a rationale rather than a routine of its own.
The principle itself carries no risk. Practices justified by it, such as forceful pulling or striking the face, have their own risks and are covered on their own pages.

angle.text: Wolff's law, the real principle that bone remodels to the loads it carries, is the logic behind mewing, chewing and pulling practices aimed at a stronger jaw and cheekbones. Applying it to adult facial bone with these methods has not been tested.

lead: Wolff's law states that bone in a healthy animal adapts to the loads placed on it, becoming denser and stronger under greater loading and weaker under less [1][2]. It is named for the German surgeon and anatomist Julius Wolff (1836-1902), whose 1892 book Das Gesetz der Transformation der Knochen set out the idea [2]. In looksmaxxing communities, 'Wolff's law' is cited as the reason that mewing, chewing, thumb pulling and similar practices are said to reshape the face.

Scientists now generally prefer the term bone functional adaptation: reviewers note that Wolff's original mathematical formulation has been discredited while the broader concept of adaptation to loading is supported by much experimental and observational data [3]. No published study has tested whether tongue posture or other do-it-yourself facial loading remodels the facial skeleton.

Theoretical basis for mewing, chewing, pulling, bonesmashing

paras: When loading on a bone increases, the bone remodels over time to resist it; when loading decreases, it loses density. Reduced loading, for example in astronauts under microgravity, leads to bone loss [2]. Only cyclic loading is described as inducing bone formation [2].

Wolff's concept built on earlier work, and Harold Frost later refined it as the mechanostat and the Utah paradigm, which propose strain thresholds. In one formulation, strains below about 50 microstrain accompany the largest disuse effects, while strains above about 1500 microstrain tend to turn on bone modeling that adds and reshapes bone [4][5]. A reviewer for clinicians argues that remodeling alone can remove or conserve bone but not add it, with modeling responsible for adding bone [4].

Remodeling works through mechanotransduction, in which cells convert mechanical signals into biochemical ones. Osteocytes, the most abundant bone cells, are particularly sensitive to fluid flow caused by loading and signal other cells [2]. Mechanically sensitive proteins such as PIEZO1 regulate bone homeostasis through osteoblast and osteoclast signalling in mouse research [6].
No studies found testing Wolff's law or bone loading as applied to do-it-yourself facial reshaping through tongue posture, chewing, pulling or striking.

Studies of bone adaptation in general include reviews written for orthodontic clinicians, which list the mandible and maxilla among load-bearing bones [5], and anthropological reviews supporting bone functional adaptation [3]. A clinical study correlated wrist loads with distal radius tilt in 30 wrists. These do not address facial change from home practices.

Proponents of mewing and related practices argue that facial bones are shaped by forces applied over time. One forum guide lists as premises that facial structure is moulded by forces, that facial sutures never fuse, and that forward growth of the maxilla is the goal. Critics in the same discussions and orthodontic bodies say these claims have not been demonstrated; the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence mewing reshapes the jaw [7].

lore.intro: 'Wolff's law' is invoked in looksmaxxing forums as scientific backing for mewing, chewing, pulling and bonesmashing, often with the argument that facial sutures never fuse.
